ATP generation by different processes
1. Substrate-Level Phosphorylation: Direct transfer of a phosphate group
from a high-energy substrate to ADP, forming ATP.
•Examples:
• Glycolysis: generating 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
• Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle): 1 ATP (or GTP) per turn.
2. Oxidative Phosphorylation: Involves the electron transport chain (ETC)
and chemiosmosis, similar to eukaryotic cells but occurring in the plasma
membrane in bacteria. 28-34 ATP per glucose molecule, depending on the
efficiency of the ETC. Electrons derived from NADH and FADH2 pump protons
(H+) across the membrane, creating a proton gradient.
3. Photophosphorylation (in Photosynthetic Bacteria): Some bacteria,
such as purple and green sulfur bacteria, generate ATP using light energy.
depending on the light intensity and specific bacterial species.
•Steps:
• Light energy excites electrons in photosynthetic pigments, which are
transferred through an electron transport chain.
• This process also creates a proton gradient, similar to oxidative
phosphorylation.
• Protons flow back through ATP synthase to generate ATP.

A lipid panel measures five different types of lipids from a blood sample,
including:
• Total cholesterol: This is your overall cholesterol level - the
combination of LDL-C, VLDL-C and HDL-C.
• Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol: This is the type of
cholesterol that's known as "bad cholesterol." It can collect in your
blood vessels and increase your risk of cardiovascular disease.
• Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) cholesterol: This is a type of
cholesterol that's usually present in very low amounts when the blood
sample is a fasting samples since it's mostly comes from food you've
recently eaten. An increase in this type of cholesterol in a fasting
sample may be a sign of abnormal lipid metabolism.
• High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol: This is the type of
cholesterol that's known as "good cholesterol." It helps decrease the
build-up of LDL in your blood vessels.
• Triglycerides: This is a type of fat from the food we eat. Excess amounts
of triglycerides in your blood are associated with cardiovascular disease
and pancreatic inflammation.

important substances, but too much of it in the blood can clog and

carry cholesterol to the liver, where it is removed from the body.

needed. If there is too much, it can block blood vessels and cause
other health problems such as abdominal pain and pancreatitis.
